source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Closest direct LLM test of Kitcher's idea. Four Claude Opus 4.6 agents sharing only a score leaderboard crowd onto the leader's approach. A per-direction board with priority-style credit spreads them out.
numbers: Leaderboard-only groups: 3 of 4 agents in one direction for most of the run; whole thirds of a run in one direction. Last-third HHI baseline vs Discovery: 1.00 vs 0.66 (Signal Proc), 1.00 vs 0.36 (Circle-Pack), 0.82 vs 0.29 (Erdos Overlap). 9 tasks, 3 runs per configuration, best of 3 reported.
quote: Agents that share only a score tend to follow the leader and converge onto one approach.
limits: Single-lab preprint (Oct 2026), not peer reviewed. Best-of-3 reporting, one model family, authors built both the system and the verifier.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S3 open mode: code labels each attempt with a direction, tracks per-direction yield, and allocates untried directions.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Headline result against the reproduced shared-leaderboard system (same model, same 4-agent budget, no internet, no grader reading except Kernel).
numbers: 6 wins, 1 tie, 2 losses over 9 tasks. Kernel 1095 vs 1138 cycles (lower is better); Polyominoes 91.78 vs 80.55 (prior SOTA 87.0); Signal Proc 0.7904 vs 0.7718; Erdos 0.380984 vs 0.381264. Reached the baseline's final best at eval 202 vs 594 on Kernel. Passes 1103 at eval 275, against 596 evals used before.
limits: Margins on Circle-Pack and EPLB lie beyond the third decimal. No variance reported. Cited published numbers came from runs with web and grader access, so only partly comparable.
agent_relevance: Spreading effort over directions beat pure exploitation on most tasks at equal compute.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Adding agents alone gave no gain. The 4-agent shared-leaderboard baseline beat the single agent on only 3 of 9 tasks, so the gain came from the allocation rule, not head count.
numbers: 4-agent baseline beats single agent on 3 of 9 tasks.
limits: Same single-lab caveats.
agent_relevance: More parallel attempts do not mean more coverage. Coverage needs an explicit allocation rule.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: The gain comes from directions the baseline never entered. A verifier relabelled all submissions by direction.
numbers: Discovery opened 68 directions vs 41 for the baseline; after the first third, 34 vs 15. Discovery-only directions: Kernel 25 (7 produced records), Polyominoes 8 (4), Signal 6 (4), Circle-Pack 4 (1), Erdos 6 (4). Kernel and Polyominoes gain 100% from Discovery-only records. The 91.78 Polyominoes record came from sa-shrink-boundary-removal, opened at eval 33. Champion directions opened at eval 62/100, 34/40, 58/60.
limits: Labels come from an LLM reading diffs (Opus 4.6). No inter-rater check seen.
agent_relevance: Late-opened directions produced the winners. A schedule that stops opening directions early would have missed them.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: The priority rule in code: credit is earned only against a direction's own best, so a lagging direction keeps its agents and still sets local records.
numbers: Local records (direction bests short of global best), Discovery vs baseline: 9 vs 0 (Signal), 4 vs 0 (Circle-Pack), 15 vs 4 (Erdos). After the Signal champion's first global record, 76% of the remaining 38 evals went to it.
limits: Mechanism described, but no ablation removes the credit rule alone.
agent_relevance: Per-direction credit against own best is a cheap, code-checkable analogue of Kitcher's priority rule. Candidate for S3.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Allocation formula: yield (shrunken mean credit per eval) plus a UCB-like bonus c*ln N/(n_all+1), plus a NEW arm that prices opening one more direction from how fast past new directions paid off. Seats go in proportion to potential (largest remainder). Advisory only; the agent decides.
numbers: At most 2 agents per direction; claim check rejects duplicate methods; each agent gets a distinct direction in round 1; after 5 scored evals without a personal best a Diagnose block fires. NEW estimate equals y+ before any opening and y+/(j+1) after j fruitless openings.
limits: Constants are task-normalised, no published sweep. Advisory board means agents may ignore it.
agent_relevance: Concrete spec for the code that allocates untried directions: bandit bonus, option value of a new direction, cap per direction.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Cost of spreading effort: on two tasks Discovery lost. Opening more directions does not guarantee finding the one with headroom.
numbers: LLM-SQL: 7 directions vs 2 for baseline; 15% of evals in directions that never produced a record; best 0.732704 vs baseline 0.733963 vs single agent 0.735769. Txn Sched: Discovery 4566 vs single agent 4608 (baseline 4367).
limits: Authors' explanation for Txn Sched (a single agent keeps the whole process history) is a conjecture, untested.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for S3: breadth helps when headroom is spread over many mechanisms; one deep direction favours one continuous line. Budget a depth phase too.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
finding: Authors tie their rule to the human literature: Kitcher 1990 (spread by credit), Weisberg and Muldoon 2009 (followers crowd one peak), Kuhn's essential tension. They say islands and MAP-Elites hard-code the division, while score-sharing agents leave it to each agent alone.
numbers: Comparison table: fixed evolutionary search vs autonomous multi-agent evolution vs Coral Discovery.
limits: Mapping to the philosophy models is by analogy. No formal test of Kitcher's predictions.
agent_relevance: Shows the Kitcher and Weisberg-Muldoon frame is now used by AI builders as a design principle.

source: Qu et al. (2026) CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery (COLM 2026)
finding: Four autonomous agents sharing memory beat one agent on hard tasks, and beat best-of-4 independent runs, so gains are not only extra compute.
numbers: Kernel Eng 1103 vs 1350 cycles (18.3% gain; 596 vs 56 evals); Polyominoes 84.2 vs 80.2 (+4.99%); Circle-Pack +7.9%; Signal Proc +2.91%. Co-evolution vs best of 4 independent runs: Kernel 1103 vs 1180; Polyominoes 84.2 vs 80.8; Txn Sched 4694 vs 4629. Open-source stack (MiniMax M2.5 + OpenCode) also improves on most tasks.
limits: Single runs per cell. Gains uneven (MMD-16-2 only +0.15%). Single agent has a higher per-eval improvement rate.
agent_relevance: Parallel agents with a shared record add value beyond sampling. Coverage is what matters, not count.

source: Qu et al. (2026) CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery (COLM 2026)
finding: Exploration diversity measured by keyword overlap of attempt titles: the four agents cover different ground.
numbers: Mean pairwise Jaccard overlap 0.43 (Kernel Eng) and 0.31 (Polyominoes). More than half of each agent's strategy vocabulary is unique.
limits: Keyword proxy for strategy is crude.
agent_relevance: A cheap diversity metric (title keyword Jaccard) that code can compute for S3.

source: Qu et al. (2026) CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery (COLM 2026)
finding: Cross-agent building is productive: 36% of Kernel attempts used another agent's commit as parent and improved 17% of the time vs 9% overall. 66% of new records had a cross-agent parent.
numbers: Polyominoes: 12% direct code transfer, 50% vs 19% improvement rate; 87% of rounds referenced others' notes.
limits: Correlational. Agents choose which commits to build on.
agent_relevance: Division of labour works only with sharing. Pure independence loses cross-fertilisation; pure sharing loses spread.

source: Qu et al. (2026) CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery (COLM 2026)
finding: Ablation: removing notes and skills (knowledge accumulation) hurts a single agent.
numbers: Kernel Eng 1350 to 1601 cycles (18.6% regression); Polyominoes 80.2 to 77.3; Txn Sched 4566 to 4444.
limits: Three stress tasks, single runs.
agent_relevance: Written records of what failed (a 'what NEVER worked' folder) help avoid re-entering dead directions.

source: Qu et al. (2026) CORAL: Towards Autonomous Multi-Agent Evolution for Open-Ended Discovery (COLM 2026)
finding: Heartbeat design: Pivot prompt fires after 5 non-improving evals, Reflect every eval, Consolidate every 10 evals. Which direction to take is left to the agent, not code.
numbers: Pivot trigger is 5 non-improving evals.
limits: Heartbeats are timing rules, not allocation rules. Not ablated alone in the text read.
agent_relevance: Plateau-triggered pivot fits our G1 (doubt only on a signal), unlike a fixed schedule.

source: Liu, Ruhrberg Estevez, Bentley, van der Schaar (2025) Hypothesis Hunting with Evolving Networks of Autonomous Scientific Agents (ASCollab)
finding: Frames a field as a Weisberg and Muldoon epistemic landscape and uses heterogeneous LLM agent personas (explore vs exploit, independent vs collaborative stances) to keep coverage broad. Cites Hong and Page 2004 as the reason.
numbers: N=16 agents, T=40 rounds, 40 ReAct steps per session, GPT-4o. Top 25 findings scored by one domain expert on novelty and quality (1-5).
limits: One expert rater, personas generated by the same LLM, single run, GPT-4o only.
agent_relevance: Persona diversity is a cheap way to induce spread. Our G4 says persona samples are not independent, so use them for coverage, not for voting.

source: Liu, Ruhrberg Estevez, Bentley, van der Schaar (2025) Hypothesis Hunting with Evolving Networks of Autonomous Scientific Agents (ASCollab)
finding: Ablation against independent agents with no shared archive: independent agents converge on a narrow set of topics and duplicate each other.
numbers: In the baseline almost half of top findings overlapped substantially, so a filter was needed to get 25 unique ones. ASCollab had no duplicates in its top 25. Gene-level histograms: independent agents concentrate on few targets.
limits: No numeric novelty or quality means in the text read (figure only).
agent_relevance: Independent same-model agents re-explore the same ground. Shared record plus dedup is the fix.

source: Liu, Ruhrberg Estevez, Bentley, van der Schaar (2025) Hypothesis Hunting with Evolving Networks of Autonomous Scientific Agents (ASCollab)
finding: Agents showed distinct trajectories: some exploit and refine one idea, others test many directions.
numbers: Six most productive agents plotted; no numbers.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Fixed stances give a built-in explorer and exploiter mix, a soft division of labour.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Over-generation by one LLM collapses to few distinct ideas. A single model does not spread over idea space by itself.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.8, all-MiniLM-L6-v2). The share of non-duplicates in each new batch falls and the cumulative count plateaus. About 5% unique.
limits: One generator model, NLP topics, 0.8 threshold set by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Sampling more from one model does not open new directions. Directions must be imposed by code (distinct claims, dedup).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Human study of 100+ NLP researchers: LLM ideas were rated more novel than human ideas, yet LLMs lack diversity as a set.
numbers: 298 unique reviews from 79 reviewers.
limits: I read the setup and the diversity section closely, not every statistic.
agent_relevance: Per-idea novelty can look good while coverage is poor. Measure set diversity, not just single quality.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: AlphaEvolve hard-codes spread with MAP-Elites plus island populations; the LLM only mutates programs.
numbers: Ablations on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers: full method beats no evolution, no context in prompt, no meta-prompt evolution, small base LLM only, no full-file evolution. Three seeds per setting.
limits: Curves only in figures; I did not extract exact numbers.
agent_relevance: Hard-coded spreading of 2025; Coral Discovery argues for an adaptive one.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended and Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
finding: ShinkaEvolve uses island subpopulations (island-best never migrates), embedding novelty rejection (similarity above 0.95 rejected) and bandit selection of which LLM to call.
numbers: New circle-packing SOTA with 150 samples. Ablations: weighted parent sampling beats hill climbing (which plateaus early) and best-of-N; novelty rejection with an LLM novelty judge strongly beats no rejection; bandit ensemble beats fixed ensemble and single GPT-5-nano.
limits: Ablation sizes visible only in figures.
agent_relevance: Code-level dedup of near-duplicate proposals stops two attempts landing in the same direction.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity (COLM 2025)
finding: Single models give few distinct answers to repeated queries; bigger models are less diverse than smaller ones in the same family.
numbers: 20 leading models; most produce on average fewer than 3 distinct responses in 10 queries; Gemma 2-2B and Llama 3.2-1B were most diverse. In-context regeneration raises diversity but does not close the gap to humans.
limits: Equivalence classes from a classifier; utility from a reward model.
agent_relevance: Resampling one model is a weak way to spread effort over approaches. Do not rely on temperature.

source: Jiang et al. (2025/2026) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Homogeneity across models as well as within: different LLMs give similar answers to open-ended queries.
numbers: 70+ LMs on INFINITY-CHAT. Same-prompt pairwise embedding similarity usually above 0.8 (top-p 0.9, T=1.0). With min-p at T=2.0, 81% of pairs above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8. DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max similarity 0.82.
limits: Sentence-embedding similarity is a surface proxy. Open-ended chat queries, not research search.
agent_relevance: A team of different models is less independent than hoped. Assign directions by code, not model variety.

source: Zhang et al. (2025/2026) Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
finding: Prompt-only fix for mode collapse: ask the model to verbalize several responses with probabilities.
numbers: Creative-writing diversity up 1.6x to 2.1x over direct prompting; human evaluation up 25.7%; recovers 66.8% of base-model diversity; more capable models gain more.
limits: Creative writing and dialogue, not correct-answer search. Quality effect varies by variant.
agent_relevance: Cheap way to make one model list distinct candidate directions before code picks which to try.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Debate among different models beats debate among copies of one model.
numbers: GSM8K after 4 rounds: Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 7Bx8 + PaLM 2-M = 91%; 3 x Gemini-Pro = 82%; individual starts 78%, 64%, 70%; ASDiv 94%.
limits: Single-author journal report, small benchmarks, answer-voting task, not search.
agent_relevance: Supports different backbones for independence; see the next line for the sceptical evidence.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Systematic test: five multi-agent debate methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 models often fail to beat single-agent chain-of-thought and self-consistency despite more compute. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: Heter-SoM improves SoM-average by 6.4%; Heter-EoT improves EoT-average by 8.2%; heterogeneous MAD beats CoT-average by up to 5.8%.
limits: Heterogeneity tested with a two-model pool. Gain comes from questions one model got right and the other wrong.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: agreement among same-model agents is not extra evidence. Spread needs different models or forced different approaches.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
finding: Co-Scientist generates, debates and evolves hypotheses in an Elo tournament, with a Proximity agent that builds a similarity graph for clustering, de-duplication and exploring the hypothesis landscape.
numbers: 203 research goals; Elo of top hypotheses rises over ten time buckets as compute is spent; 15 expert-curated hard goals.
limits: Elo is LLM-judged. I did not read the expert and lab validation parts in detail.
agent_relevance: A concrete LLM-agent use of a similarity graph to avoid duplicate directions. Code-friendly.

source: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other (NeurIPS 2026, MACE)
finding: Reports that LLM agents explore their peers poorly (myopic, polarized interaction) and proposes MACE, a structured peer selection framework.
numbers: No numbers on the page fetched (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only, not read in full.
agent_relevance: Same warning: LLMs left alone do not spread effort.

source: From Individual to Social Imitation: How Communities Expand Organizational Search (2026)
finding: Agent-based model of organizational search where communities distill portable strategies and organizations judge fit, called a division of cognitive labor.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Says gains come from evaluating a small candidate set and may hold when only a minority can evaluate.
limits: Not about LLMs. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A minority of evaluators can lift population performance: a hint for a single evaluator step in code.

source: Search-result snippet on critiques of Weisberg and Muldoon 2009 (Himmelreich and others)
finding: Search snippet says later work found programming errors and weak representational adequacy and derivational robustness in the Weisberg-Muldoon model, and argued it did not show epistemic reasons for dividing labour.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Snippet only, not opened. Other angles should open the original replications.
agent_relevance: Do not use the 2009 headline (mavericks beat followers) as settled support for S3.
